newsitem.title: USA: FORD, GM POST HIGHER SECOND QUARTER PROFITS.
newsitem.headline: FORD, GM POST HIGHER SECOND QUARTER PROFITS.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. reported the highest quarterly profit in U.S. corporate history Wednesday while General Motors Corp. overcame two strikes to post stronger-than-expected earnings for the second quarter.
Both automakers reaped the benefits of cost cutting in their core car and truck operations.

Ford said it earned $2.53 billion in the quarter, surpassing Exxon's Corp.'s fourth quarter 1996 profit of $2.49 billion as the highest on record. The results, which equalled $2.06 a share, rose 33 percent from the $1.9 billion, or $1.56 a share, Ford earned a year earlier.

GM was not far behind with profits of $2.1 billion in the quarter, up 11 percent from the $1.9 billion a year ago. GM's biggest quarter, when it earned $2.15 billion, came in the first quarter of 1995, before it spun off Electronic Data Systems Corp. last year.

Strikes at GM assembly plants in Oklahoma City and Pontiac, Mich., cut GM's profits by $490 million, but one-time gains of $421 million related to Hughes Electronics Corp. and the sale of Avis Europe largely offset that.
The Ford profit included a net gain of $100 million from the initial public offering of its Hertz rental car unit.

"For both Ford and GM, these were very powerful earnings in a tough environment -- a masterful achievement," said Scott Merlis, an auto analyst in Westport, Conn. "The strength in the earnings is a result of good old-fashioned cost cutting."
The results far outshined the 53 percent drop in profits Chrysler Corp. reported last week, largely because of a strike at an engine plant and higher spending on incentives to lure buyers.
Ford said it cut automotive costs by $1 billion, helping to push worldwide automotive profits to $1.7 billion from $1.1 billion on a modest 3.8 percent rise in production.

In the United States, Ford also got a huge boost from strong sales of its full-size Ford Expedition and Lincoln Navigator sport utility vehicles, which analysts estimate bring in profits of more than $10,000 each.
In fact, one analyst dubbed the Wayne, Mich., factory that builds the massive trucks "The Bureau of Printing and Engraving," after the federal money printing agency.

"The model mix issue is a very powerful phenomenon," said Furman Selz analyst Maryann Keller. "As long as Americans continue to want to buy giant trucks to go to the grocery store in, this is the best of all possible worlds for them."

Despite the good results, Ford stock fell $1.75 to $40.375, largely as investors took profits after a recent runup ahead of the earnings report. Ford beat analysts' average estimates but Burnham Securities analyst David Healy said its profits were a bit below the "whisper number" on Wall Street that traders circulate before an earnings report.
Ford Chief Financial Officer John Devine also cautioned that Ford's cost cutting would slow down, although he predicted continued profit gains.
"We can improve our profitability, even if there isn't a substantial volume growth," he told a news conference.
Wall Street greeted GM's performance more favourably. GM stock rose as high as $56 before closing at $54.375, up 12.5 cents on the New York Stock Exchange.
GM Chief Financial Officer J. Michael Losh said cost cutting was also a driving force behind GM's profit gain.
"It's the way we were able to make money despite lower volume," he said.

GM's production fell 3.2 percent to 2,243,000 vehicles, with about 96,000 units lost to the strikes. GM's North American operations earned $474 million during the quarter, compared with $705 million a year earlier.
Losh also hinted that the nearly three-month-old truck walkout in Pontiac affecting 5,800 workers would be resolved soon because negotiators "are down to a very few issues."
The strikes also contributed to another decline in U.S. market share for GM, to 30.5 percent for the quarter, from 32 percent a year earlier.
But Losh, long dogged by questions about GM's falling market share, vowed that by year-end GM's share will be higher than the 31 percent it held in 1996.
